5.2 What would they look like if the dimmer spots on the cell surface were included?

5.3 Provide the raw data behind Figure 3G-K so that other people can examine them

6.Unitarity of the 'unitary nodes'

The spots on the cell surface dimmer than the 'unitary nodes' hand-picked by the authors were indeed observed also in the FPALM image in Figure S2 of Laplante (2017). There were smaller clusters of emissions marked by arrows (pages 18 of 'problems.pdf'), which were excluded from the analysis without any reasoning.

Moreover, even within the data of the clusters that the authors believed to be 'unitary nodes', there is a clear sign of heterogeneity. The distributions of the numbers of emissions per cluster show a long tail, which contains ~30% or more clusters. This indicates that, in addition to the dimmer clusters that were not counted as 'nodes', there exist significant heterogeneities even among the hand-picked 'nodes'. It is not clear what "Nodes in the tail were seen only in long reconstructions (25 s), not in short reconstructions (5 s)." (page E5880 Laplante (2017)) means without the real data for the short reconstructions.

The concept of 'unitary node' might be supported if the brighter spots were able to be explained as integer multiples of unit intensity. In Akamatsu (2017), the authors argued that the distributions of fluoresce intensity of the interface nodes can be better fitted by multiple Gaussian distributions than by continuous log-normal distributions. However, the fitting was done by setting the amplitudes, SDs, and means for each of the Gaussian distributions as free parameters (9 or 12 parameters for 3 or 4 Gaussians, respectively). This is simply wrong since there must be restrictions both on the means and SDs. The mean and SD of the n'th peak (m_n and s_n, respectively) should follow m_n = m_1 x n and sd_n = sd_1 x square root of n. A simple comparison of the goodness of fit with the other distribution that has only a limited degree of freedom (the log-normal distribution has only 2 parameters) is non-sense. The comparison between the statistical models should have been done based on an appropriate estimator such as the Akaike information criterion (AIC) (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akaike_information_criterion). With a simulation https://www.dropbox.com/s/suti2gz9ovgmfyw/histogram.pdf?dl=0, Reviewer 2 raised a valid example of artificial appearance of multimodality from a log-normal distribution.

Considering all the points discussed so far, i.e.,

-Unexplained exclusion of smaller clusters in the analysis of FPALM data (Laplante (2017))

-The long tail towards the bigger clusters even among the selected '(unitary) nodes' (Laplante (2017))

-Inappropriate statistical analysis of the distribution of the intensity of the nodes with a long tail (Akamatsu (2017))

-The intensity of the spots picked by the authors as 'unitary nodes' from the Airyscan images doesn't seem to follow a normal distribution (Figure 2D and Figure 3G),

evidence for the 'unitary node' is pretty weak. We can't exclude a possibility that there is no such thing as 'unitary node' but the nodes are rather amorphous aggregates of proteins as illustrated on page 20 of 'problems.pdf'. A critical re-examination of the author's own past data must be done.

7.Nature of the dotty cytoplasmic signal

The authors responded, "The processing of Airyscan images increases the contrast of these dim inhomogeneities". It remains as a black box what image processing was done as the only information provided is "To increase signal-to-noise ratio and resolution, acquired images were processed by 3D Airyscan filter strength 7.0 with Zen Black software."

7.2 Does this processing preserve the linearity of the fluorescence signal?

7.3 Why are the grayscale levels so small? Only a range 0 to <~30 in 0-65535 grayscale levels was used.

It would not be necessary to reanalyze all strains/images this way, but perhaps just wild type and some cdc25-22 cells to establish a similar scaling trend by both methods.

Issue 2 Variability of the cytoplasmic signal and measurement of the node intensity and the node number

The reviewer pointed out the difficulties in handling the background signal (1) large fluctuation and (2) systematic decrease towards the cell tips.

The regions closer to the equatorial zone used in this version are better than the regions near tips, addressing the point 2 to some extent although, as was previously mentioned, the cytoplasmic signals are even higher in the perinuclear region next to the equatorial cortex.

To draw a conclusion that the fluctuation is small, the line scans were shown in Figure R2. The authors claimed that the signal along the cell edge (green) containing the nodes is much higher (51{plus minus}21 AU, mean{plus minus}sd) than the cytoplasm (14{plus minus}5 AU). This itself is correct. However, this doesn't support that the background fluctuation is small relative to the intensity of the 'unitary nodes' since the major peaks (60~90 AU) on the green profile in Figure R2B correspond to the clusters of the many 'unitary nodes' (please refer to page1 of problems2.pdf). The spot measured as a 'unitary node' (ROI 0025-0270-0044, arrow) corresponds to a minor peak of ~30 AU, which is comparable to the fluctuations of the blue profile. They brought the intensity of the clusters of 'unitary node' when discussing the intensity of individual 'unitary nodes' relative to the background fluctuation.

The authors tried to explain the difference between their claim and the reviewer's analysis "Our measurement of background fluorescence (blue curve, in Figure R2B) differed from the reviewer's analysis in two ways: (1) They did not subtract the background outside cells from the image, so the background intensity is higher in their analysis; and (2) their ROI extended outside the tips of the cell, where the fluorescence is lower." In addition to the above issue, both the remarks miss the point. As to (1), firstly, subtraction of the common background (outside of the cell) doesn't influence the comparison between the peak of the 'unitary node' and the fluctuation of the cytoplasmic background. Secondly, in the previous review, when discussing the mean levels of the cytoplasmic background, they were standardized with the background outside the cell set to 0 and the mean node intensity set to 1 and pointed out that the cytoplasmic background levels vary 33% to 64% of the mean intensity of the 'unitary nodes' depending on the location with large spreads. As to (2), the line ROI was simply set from one end to another end of the outline of the cell defined by the authors, which seems to be overlapping with the other cell on the righthand side.

Issue 3 Dimmer spots on the cell surface

A concern was raised about the criteria to spot the 'unitary nodes' by picking up just slightly dimmer spots observed next to the 'unitary nodes' on the equatorial cortex, which were not counted by the authors. The authors responded to this by measuring the dim specks that are found everywhere and are easily distinguishable from the 'unitary nodes' (~170 AU, ~15 times dimmer). However, the key point was how one can define criteria that distinguish those just slightly dimmer spots the reviewer picked up from the authors' 'unitary nodes'. This was because, if it was difficult, (1) this would question the concept of the 'unitary node' and (2) this would affect the average intensity of the 'unitary nodes' and hence the node counts. The authors' argument using much dimmer cytoplasmic specks is out of focus. The authors' argument based on the minimal contribution of the dim specks to the overall signal in the broad band doesn't address these problems.

They also made comments on the spots the reviewer picked up. 5 of 8 spots were rejected because "Spot x is small and the fluorescence is limited to 2-3 Z-slices" However, these are ad-hoc and highly subjective criteria as we still find in the Methods section "To qualify as a unitary node, a spot had to satisfy two conditions: (1) the fluorescence of a spot was present within a circle 12 pixels (~0.5 μm) in diameter; (2) the fluorescence of a spot was present in 7 or fewer consecutive Z-slices. with a peak in the middle slice and diminishing towards both sides.". Note the terminologies, "within" and "7 or fewer consecutive Z-slices". They also commented on Spot 1 "Spot 1 looked like two spots together in both the X-Y and X-Z-slices, so we did not count it as a node." However, this is also the case for the ROI 0016-0244-0082 on the same z-slices, ROI 0018-0306-0104 and 0019-0249-0116, which have irregular, non-circular appearances (pages 8-10 of problem.pdf shared previously).

The node is a structure with a diameter of less than 100 nm. The observed spots are the convolution of the geometry of fluorescent proteins and the point spread function of the microscope, followed by deconvolution. The major factor that determines the size of a spot is the intensity of the fluorescence. The exclusion based on the size of the spot is almost equivalent to the exclusion by the fluorescence intensity, which is proportional to the number of the tagged molecules.

Issue 4 Statistical test for normal distribution

It was admitted that the proper test rejected that the distribution of the intensity of the 'unitary nodes' follows a Gaussian distribution unless an additional selection is introduced. This is consistent with the uncertainty and subjectiveness of the criteria for the 'unitary nodes' discussed above. Anyway, the reason for the change in the number of cells needs to be clarified. Does the original dataset pass the normality test after the same manipulation (cutting the long tail)?

It is difficult to understand why the authors insist on the normal distribution. Akamatsu (2017) showed a distribution of Blt1 with a similar spread, which was fit with multiple Gaussian. Figure 2D can easily be fit with multiple Gaussians as well (page 2 of the Reviewer problems2.pdf)

In this version, there are two different Figure 2D histograms, one on page 9 and the other on page 55. They are different in bins centered on 3000 and 3500 (arrows in page 3 of problems2.pdf) in addition to those centered on 5000, 5500, 6000, and 6500. This difference must influence the Gaussian fitting with the nodes whose intensity was less than 4600 A.U. However, the two curves of Gaussian fitting seem to be identical (both annotated as "2300{plus minus}900"). Something is wrong here.

Issue 5 Distributions of fluorescence intensities of small nodes in mutant strains

The authors claim that the distributions in the current Figure 3G follow a normal distribution based on the Shapiro-Wilk test, attributing this change to the new analysis with the background ROIs adjacent to the node broad band. However, the number of the cells analyzed is quite different from the previous versions (24 cells to 18 cells in an extreme case). Why were some data silently omitted? Can we get the same results with the original set of cells?

Issue 6 Unitarity of the 'unitary nodes'

The authors accepted that, by FPALM, they had detected clusters smaller (or less number of localized emissions) than the 'unitary nodes' but excluded them from their analysis. They rationalize the omission of these smaller clusters by arguing (1) they are distributed across the entire surface and (2) some of them are not on the flat surface. However, these arguments are weak. As for (1), it is true that there are small clusters across the entire cell surface (Laplante 2016 Figure 1A, an enhanced image on page 4 of problems2.pdf). However, they are much smaller/dimmer than those the reviewer previously spotted in Figure S2E, and the similar ones in Figure 1A found in the equatorial zone with roughly about a half the density of those marked as the 'unitary nodes' (indicated by arrows on page 4 of problems2.pdf). Much smaller clusters everywhere are not a good reason to exclude the slightly smaller clusters (with about a half the number of localized emissions of the 'unitary node') found next to the 'unitary node' in the equatorial cell cortex. As for (2), the dimmer clusters spotted are within 500 nm from those scored as nodes containing one or two 'unitary nodes'. Is the curvature of the cell surface so steep?

results.result: Wild-type fission yeast cells have approximately 190 single cytokinesis nodes early in mitosis, with single node fluorescence intensity of 2300 ± 900 AU following a normal distribution. About 85% of these nodes are incorporated into contractile rings.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C49, C50, and C51 are well-supported by Airyscan microscopy measurements, statistical validation (Shapiro-Wilk test, Z-score), and quantitative fluorescence analysis shown in Figures 2D and 2E. The methodology for counting nodes by dividing total fluorescence by average single node intensity is sound, and the statistical tests confirm the normal distribution assumption.

results.result: The number of cytokinesis nodes scales linearly with cell volume (slope ~0.7 nodes/µm³) across multiple strains with varying cell sizes, but does not correlate with cell diameter. The rga4Δ mutant cells deviate from this trend with fewer nodes than expected for their volume.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C59-C63 are supported by linear regression analysis (p<0.0001, R²=0.5) across 125 cells from multiple strains shown in Figure 3H-I. The deviation of rga4Δ cells is documented and the lack of correlation with diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) strengthens the volume-specific relationship. Statistical significance is properly reported.

results.result: The local concentration of Pom1 at the plasma membrane in the broad band region does not vary significantly across cells with different sizes and node numbers, indicating that local Pom1 concentration does not control cytokinesis node number during the G2/M transition.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C70-C72 are supported by quantitative measurements across five strains with fivefold size variation (Figure 4C-D) showing no significant correlation (p=0.07, R²=0.03). The linear regression analysis properly demonstrates the lack of relationship between local Pom1 concentration and node number.

results.result: Artificially varying total cellular Pom1 concentration using the nmt81 promoter increases cell length, local Pom1 concentration at the membrane, and cytokinesis node number above the baseline of ~190, while single node intensity and broad band width remain constant. This results in higher node density and a smaller fractional broad band width.
results.evaluation: Claims C10, C73-C82 are supported by systematic measurements across different Pom1 expression levels (Figure 5). Linear regressions show significant correlations for cell length (p<0.0001, R²=0.5), membrane Pom1 (p<0.0001, R²=0.7), and node number (p=0.0017, R²=0.3), while broad band width shows no correlation (p=0.3). The experimental design using the nmt81 promoter is appropriate.

results.result: Artificially increasing total cellular Cdr2 concentration reduces cell length at division but does not change broad band width, resulting in increased node numbers above the basal level of ~190 and higher node density.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87, C89 are supported by measurements using the nmt81 promoter system (Figure 6). Significant correlations are shown for cell length (p<0.0001, R²=0.6) and node number (p<0.0001, R²=0.6), while broad band width shows no correlation (p=0.9). The conclusion that Cdr2 can drive node numbers above baseline is justified by the data.

results.result: Airyscan microscopy with ~140 nm resolution resolves dim single cytokinesis nodes better than conventional confocal microscopy, producing brighter and narrower images of contractile rings and retrieving higher spatial frequencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 are supported by direct comparison between Airyscan and confocal imaging (Figure 1) and Fast Fourier transform analysis showing superior frequency retrieval. The technical specifications of Airyscan are well-established, and the visual and quantitative comparisons validate the improved resolution.

results.result: In freely cycling cells (excluding cdc25-22), both node density and broad band width increase with node number and cell size. In contrast, cdc25-22 mutant cells expand broad band width proportionally to node number without increasing density.
results.evaluation: Claims C64, C65, C108 are supported by data in Figure 3J-K showing different scaling behaviors. The distinction between cdc25-22 and other strains is clearly documented with appropriate statistical analysis. The mechanistic explanation for cdc25-22 behavior (arrested at G2/M) is reasonable.

results.result: Different strains incorporate varying fractions of Blt1 from cytokinesis nodes into contractile rings (40-90%), with cdc25-22 mutant cells showing particularly low incorporation (~50% in largest cells) for Blt1 but normal incorporation for Myo2.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C69, C120-C121 are supported by fluorescence measurements in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2E. The differential incorporation of Blt1 vs Myo2 in cdc25-22 cells is a novel observation properly documented with quantitative data. Statistical significance is established (p=0.035 for wild-type comparison).

results.result: Temperature-sensitive mutants and deletion mutants produce cells with altered dimensions: wee1-50 cells are half the length of wild-type; cdc25-22 cells are twice as long; rga4Δ cells are shorter but wider; rga2Δ cells are narrower but normal length.
results.evaluation: Claims C52-C57 are supported by quantitative measurements in Figure 3 and are consistent with known functions of these genes. The measurements include appropriate sample sizes and standard deviations. These phenotypes are well-established in the literature and properly reproduced here.

results.result: Cell size is the dominant determinant of the basal number of cytokinesis nodes (~190 in wild-type), with Pom1 and Cdr2 modulating this number through their effects on cell size during interphase and their concentrations during mitosis.
results.evaluation: Claims C90, C91, C94, C95 represent the central mechanistic model supported by the scaling data (Figure 3H), the Pom1/Cdr2 manipulation experiments (Figures 5-6), and integration with prior literature. The model is consistent with all experimental observations and properly distinguishes basal from modulated node numbers.

results.result: Pom1 regulates node localization and cell size through a phosphorylation cascade: Pom1 phosphorylates and inhibits Cdr2 (affecting oligomerization and membrane binding), Cdr2 phosphorylates and inhibits Wee1, and Wee1 phosphorylates Cdk1. As cells grow, Pom1's influence diminishes, contributing to mitotic entry.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C100 are well-supported by multiple citations to prior work establishing this pathway. The current study's observations of Pom1 distribution (Figure 4) and effects of Pom1 overexpression (Figure 5) are consistent with this established mechanism. This represents integration of prior knowledge with new observations.

results.result: Overexpression of Cdr2 increases node numbers by mass action and promotes premature mitosis through Wee1 inhibition, resulting in short cells with densely packed nodes. Overexpression of Pom1 delays mitosis allowing cells to grow longer, with the dominant effect of cell size producing more nodes despite Cdr2 inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C104, C112 represent mechanistic interpretations of the experimental data (Figures 5-6) but are largely speculative. While the observations are solid, the proposed mechanisms involving 'mass action' and the relative contributions of different pathways are not directly tested. The authors appropriately use tentative language ('might', 'may'), but these remain hypotheses requiring further validation.

results.result: During interphase growth in wild-type cells, the Pom1 concentration remains low in a widening zone at the cell middle, while node density and number increase with cell size (except in cdc25-22 cells), and the broad band widens proportionally.
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107 are supported by the scaling data (Figure 3J-K), Pom1 distribution measurements (Figure 4C), and integration with prior literature (Bhatia et al., 2014; Pan et al., 2014). The observations extend previous findings to a wider range of cell sizes and are internally consistent.

results.result: Cell shape influences node number, with large-diameter rga4Δ cells having fewer nodes than expected for their volume despite normal node properties. These cells also show a steeper Pom1 gradient and wider Blt1 distribution.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C117 are supported by the deviation of rga4Δ cells from the volume-node number relationship (Figure 3H) and the Pom1 distribution data (Figure 4B). The observation is well-documented, though the mechanistic explanation remains incomplete. This represents a genuine exception to the volume-scaling rule.

results.result: Background on cytokinesis node biology: nodes are stoichiometric protein assemblies that serve as contractile ring precursors, form from two types of interphase nodes, mature by sequential protein accumulation, and are linked to cell size control.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C11-C24 represent established background knowledge properly cited from prior literature. These claims provide essential context but are not novel findings of this study. The citations are appropriate and the descriptions are accurate based on the referenced work.

results.result: Prior studies using various microscopy techniques estimated cytokinesis node numbers ranging from <50 to ~140, with limitations including inability to detect dim nodes, resolution constraints, and reliance on extrapolation. SMLM revealed that nodes are uniform in size but appear heterogeneous in confocal images due to clustering.
results.evaluation: Claims C25-C40 accurately summarize prior literature on node counting methods and their limitations. The citations are appropriate and the critical assessment of previous methods (including their own prior work) is fair and well-documented. This provides essential justification for the current study's approach.

results.result: Blt1 is the only protein that persists in nodes throughout the cell cycle, making it suitable as a marker. Time-lapse imaging shows nodes of all sizes condense into contractile rings over 10-12 minutes, but neither Airyscan nor confocal microscopy can resolve individual nodes within rings.
results.evaluation: Claims C42, C47, C48 are supported by citations for Blt1's unique properties and by the imaging data. The limitation regarding resolution of nodes in rings is appropriately acknowledged and consistent with the known resolution limits of these techniques compared to SMLM.

results.result: Single node fluorescence intensity is consistent (~2300 AU) across wild-type and all experimental strains tested.
results.evaluation: Claim C58 is supported by the histogram data in Figure 3G showing similar distributions across strains. Tukey's multiple comparison test confirms no significant differences (p>0.05) except for rga4Δ+HU (p=0.04), which is a minor deviation. This validates the use of a common single-node intensity for node counting across strains.

results.result: Only about half of each known node protein assembles into nodes, and cells lacking either Cdr2 or Pom1 can still form cytokinesis nodes, indicating a basal node-forming capacity independent of these kinases.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C93 are supported by appropriate citations (Akamatsu et al., 2017 for C92; multiple citations for C93). These observations from prior work are correctly interpreted to support the concept of a basal node number that can be modulated by Pom1 and Cdr2.

results.result: Two additional factors contribute to restricting nodes to the equator: an uncharacterized activity that excludes nodes from one pole in pom1Δ cells, and anillin Mid1, as mid1Δ cells have nodes spread over the entire plasma membrane.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. These represent known but incompletely understood aspects of node localization that complement the Pom1-mediated restriction mechanism. The citations are accurate and relevant.

results.result: In arrested cdc25-22 cells that continue growing, extra nodes formed after the threshold time spread out further from the edges of the broad band.
results.evaluation: Claim C111 is a speculative explanation for why cdc25-22 cells show different scaling behavior (expanding broad band width rather than increasing density). While this interpretation is reasonable given the experimental design (cells arrested at G2/M), it is not directly demonstrated. The claim represents inference rather than direct observation.

results.result: Cells overexpressing Pom1 have higher node density due to more nodes in normal-width broad bands, with increased Pom1 concentration in the cell middle suppressing broad band spreading despite increased cell length.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are supported by the data in Figures 5F-G showing constant broad band width with increased node numbers, and Figure 5B showing increased local Pom1 concentration. The observations are internally consistent and properly documented.

results.result: Most cytokinesis node proteins are initially incorporated into contractile rings, with Myo2 retained and concentrated while Mid1 and actin are lost during constriction. The observation that nodes in rings have different compositions than cytokinesis nodes suggests compositional changes during ring maturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 are supported by appropriate citations to prior work. Claim C122 is a reasonable inference from the new observation that Blt1 and Myo2 show different incorporation patterns (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), suggesting that ring nodes differ from cytokinesis nodes. This inference is logical but requires further validation.
